essays.stem: A hardware chain with six branches is considering a new cloud-based inventory system. Describe the steps you would follow to evaluate it, from identifying needs to making a recommendation.
essays.modelAnswer: I would start by defining the business need: for example, stock-outs and over-stocking because branch stock levels are not visible in real time. I would talk to branch managers, store staff and the accounts team to list the must-have and nice-to-have requirements, such as live stock levels, barcode scanning, reorder alerts and links to the accounts package. Next, I would scan the market using independent reviews, trade contacts and similar businesses, and shortlist three suitable systems. I would set evaluation criteria with weights, such as fit to requirements, total cost of ownership over three to five years, ease of use, integration, security, support in Jamaica and the supplier's stability. Each vendor would demonstrate its system with our own data, and I would contact reference customers. The best option would be tested in a short pilot at one branch with clear measures. I would also assess risks, including internet and power outages, data protection and vendor lock-in. Finally, I would write a report to the directors comparing the options and giving a justified recommendation and an implementation plan.
markingPoints: Defines the business need and gathers user requirements
Researches the market and shortlists options
Sets weighted criteria including total cost of ownership
Tests through demonstrations, references or a pilot and assesses risks
Reports with a justified recommendation

essays.stem: A law firm must choose between two ways of running its document system for the next three years. Option A: buy a server for J$1,500,000, pay J$300,000 to set it up and J$250,000 a year to maintain it. Option B: a cloud service at J$60,000 a month, with a J$150,000 set-up fee. Work out the three-year cost of each option, and recommend one, taking account of non-financial factors.
essays.modelAnswer: Option A costs J$1,500,000 to buy plus J$300,000 to set up, which is J$1,800,000, plus three years of maintenance at J$250,000, which is J$750,000. The three-year total is J$2,550,000. Option B costs J$60,000 a month for 36 months, which is J$2,160,000, plus the J$150,000 set-up fee, which gives J$2,310,000. On cost over three years, Option B is cheaper by J$240,000, and it also spreads the cost evenly, which helps cash flow. However, other factors matter. A law firm holds confidential client documents, so I would check where the cloud provider stores data, how it is encrypted, who can access it and whether it meets the data protection law. The cloud service depends on a reliable internet connection, so a backup line would be needed. Option A keeps data in the office but needs in-house IT skill, secure premises, backups and protection from power cuts. Unless the cloud provider fails the security checks, I would recommend Option B, with a strong contract on data ownership and an exit plan.
markingPoints: Option A correctly totalled at J$2,550,000
Option B correctly totalled at J$2,310,000
States that Option B is cheaper by J$240,000
Weighs security, confidentiality, internet, skills or data protection
Gives a justified recommendation with conditions

essays.stem: Explain the main risks of adopting a new technology for a small or medium business in Jamaica, and describe how each can be managed.
essays.modelAnswer: One risk is that the technology does not meet the real need, perhaps because it was chosen for its features rather than the problem. This is managed by defining requirements with users first and testing the system before buying. A second risk is cost overrun from hidden costs such as data migration, training and customisation, which a full total cost of ownership and a contingency budget help to control. Third, power cuts and weak internet in some areas can stop online systems; the business should plan backup power, a second internet connection and offline working. Fourth, cyber attacks and data breaches could harm customers and break the data protection law, so the firm should check security, use strong passwords and two-step login, train staff and keep backups. Fifth, the supplier may fail or the firm may become locked in, so the firm should check the supplier's track record and make sure the contract covers data ownership and exit. Finally, staff may resist or misuse the system; involving them early and giving training reduce this. A risk register with owners keeps these under review.
markingPoints: Identifies need or cost risks with controls
Identifies power or connectivity risks with controls
Identifies security and data protection risks with controls
Identifies supplier or lock-in risks with controls
Identifies people or change risks and uses a risk register

essays.stem: Design a weighted scoring method to compare three point-of-sale systems for a restaurant group, and explain why weighting the criteria matters.
essays.modelAnswer: First, the management team and users would agree the criteria that matter most to the restaurants. These might be functions (orders, kitchen printing, split bills and card and mobile payments), ease of use for busy servers, total cost of ownership over three years, integration with the accounts and stock systems, reliability during power or internet outages, and local support. Each criterion would get a weight that reflects its importance, with the weights adding to 100%: for example functions 25%, ease of use 20%, cost 20%, integration 15%, reliability 10% and support 10%. Each system would be scored from 1 to 10 on every criterion, using demonstrations, trials and reference calls, ideally by at least two people to reduce bias. Each score is multiplied by its weight and the results are added to give a total for each system. Weighting matters because not all criteria are equally important: without it, a cheap system with weak functions could score the same as an excellent one. The method also makes the decision clear, fair and easy to explain to the directors.
markingPoints: Relevant criteria agreed with users and managers
Weights reflect importance and total 100%
Scores based on evidence, ideally by more than one person
Correct method: score times weight, then add
Explains why weighting matters for a fair, transparent choice

essays.stem: Explain why a business should run a pilot or proof of concept before fully adopting a new technology, and describe how you would plan one.
essays.modelAnswer: A pilot or proof of concept tests a technology on a small scale before the business commits large sums. It shows whether the system really works with the firm's data, processes and staff, reveals faults and hidden costs early, and gives evidence for the final decision rather than relying on the vendor's claims. It also lets staff try the system and build confidence. To plan one, I would first set clear objectives and success measures, such as the time to process an order, error rates and user satisfaction, and record the current baseline. I would choose a typical site or team and a fixed period, for example six weeks, and agree with the vendor what will be provided and at what cost. Test data would be realistic, but personal data would be protected. I would train the pilot users, keep a log of problems and collect their feedback weekly. At the end, I would compare the results with the baseline and the success measures and recommend whether to adopt, adapt or reject the system.
markingPoints: Explains the purpose: test fit, find problems and reduce risk
Sets objectives, success measures and a baseline
Chooses a typical site, period and scope agreed with the vendor
Trains users, logs issues and gathers feedback, protecting data
Compares results and makes a decision

essays.stem: Explain the difference between purchase price and total cost of ownership, and describe the costs you would include when evaluating new human resource software for a company with 150 staff.
essays.modelAnswer: The purchase price is only what is paid to obtain the software at the start, such as the licence fee or the first year's subscription. The total cost of ownership is the full cost of having and using the system over its expected life, often three to five years, so it gives a fairer basis for comparing options. For human resource software for 150 staff, I would include licence or subscription fees for all users over the period, any GCT at the current rate, and set-up and configuration costs. I would add the cost of moving staff records from the old system, links to the payroll and accounts systems, and any new hardware or extra internet capacity. Training costs for HR staff, managers and employees, including staff time away from work, should be included. Ongoing costs include support and maintenance fees, upgrades, security measures, backups and internal staff time to manage the system. Finally, I would allow for the costs of ending the contract and moving to another system later, and a contingency for unexpected costs.
markingPoints: Defines purchase price correctly
Defines total cost of ownership over the system's life
Includes set-up, data migration and integration costs
Includes training and staff time
Includes ongoing support, upgrades, security and exit costs

essays.stem: Evaluate cloud-based software against software installed on a firm's own servers for a medium-sized insurance broker in Kingston, and make a recommendation.
essays.modelAnswer: Cloud-based software is run by the provider and reached over the internet for a regular fee. Its advantages are a low starting cost, quick set-up, automatic updates, the ability to add users easily as the firm grows, and access for staff working from different branches or from home. The provider usually handles backups and security. Its disadvantages are reliance on a good internet connection, ongoing fees that may cost more over many years, less control over where data is stored, and the risk of lock-in. Software on the firm's own servers gives more control over data and customisation, and may cost less over a long life. However, it needs a large upfront spend, in-house IT skill, secure and air-conditioned space, backup power and the firm's own backups and security, and upgrades are the firm's job. An insurance broker holds sensitive personal and financial data, so security and the data protection law are central. I would recommend the cloud option if the provider meets strict security, data location and service level standards and the firm installs a backup internet line.
markingPoints: Gives advantages of cloud software
Gives disadvantages of cloud software
Gives advantages and disadvantages of own-server software
Relates the evaluation to the broker's sensitive data and needs
Makes a recommendation with conditions

essays.stem: Set out the main sections of a report recommending a new technology to a company's board, and explain what each section should contain.
essays.modelAnswer: The report would open with an executive summary of one page or less, giving the problem, the recommended option, its cost and its main benefit, so that busy directors can grasp the decision quickly. The introduction would explain the purpose and scope of the evaluation and who was consulted. The business need section would describe the current problem and its cost, with evidence such as error rates or lost sales. The options section would describe the shortlisted technologies, including doing nothing, and the evaluation method, such as weighted criteria. The analysis section would compare the options on total cost of ownership, benefits, return on investment or payback, fit, integration, security and supplier strength, using tables, and would report pilot or reference results. The risk section would list the main risks with their likelihood, impact and controls. The recommendation would state clearly which option to adopt and why. The implementation section would outline the timeline, training, data migration, budget and how success will be measured and reviewed. Appendices would hold detailed scores and quotations.
markingPoints: Executive summary and introduction with purpose and scope
Business need with evidence
Options and evaluation method, including doing nothing
Analysis of costs, benefits and risks
Clear recommendation with implementation and review plan

essays.stem: An insurer is considering an artificial intelligence chatbot for customer service. Explain how you would evaluate it, including ethical and legal points.
essays.modelAnswer: I would start by defining what the chatbot should do, such as answering common questions about policies and claims at any hour, and how success would be measured: accuracy, the share of queries resolved, customer satisfaction and cost per contact. I would test it with real questions, including difficult and unusual ones, and check that its answers are correct and that it hands complex or sensitive cases quickly to a person. The chatbot must be clear to customers that they are talking to a machine, and it must not give misleading advice about cover, because the firm remains responsible for what it says. Personal data used or collected must be handled under the data protection law, with clear consent, secure storage and limits on how long it is kept. I would check for bias, for example whether it treats customers fairly whatever their way of writing English or their age, and make sure customers who prefer phone or face-to-face service still have that choice. I would consult staff whose jobs may change. Finally, I would run a pilot and review the results before deciding.
markingPoints: Defines purpose and success measures
Tests accuracy and hand-over to staff
Covers honesty with customers and responsibility for advice
Covers data protection and fairness or bias
Considers staff and customer choice, and pilots before deciding

essays.stem: Explain how a business should review a new technology after it has been in use for six months, and what it should do with the findings.
essays.modelAnswer: The review should compare what actually happened with what the business case promised. I would gather data on the measures set before the purchase, such as processing time, error rates, sales, costs and system uptime, and compare them with the baseline and the targets. I would check the actual costs against the budget, including any hidden costs, and work out whether the expected payback is still realistic. I would survey users and hold short group discussions to learn how easy the system is to use, which features are not being used, and what problems remain. I would also check whether the supplier is meeting the service level agreement and whether security and data protection controls are working. The findings would go in a short report to management. Problems would be turned into an action plan, for example more training, changes to settings or a discussion with the supplier. If the system is clearly failing, the business might consider its exit options. Lessons learned would be recorded so that the next technology evaluation is better.
markingPoints: Compares results with the business case, baseline and targets
Checks actual costs and payback
Gathers user feedback and checks supplier and security performance
Reports findings and turns them into actions
Records lessons for future evaluations

practical1.title: Evaluate three technology options and write a recommendation report
practical1.brief: The assessor gives your group a case pack for a made-up business (for example a group of three guest houses in Treasure Beach, a medical clinic in Spanish Town, or a hardware store chain in Mandeville) that needs a new booking, records or stock system, with fact sheets and quotations for three made-up products. As a group, evaluate the options and produce: a list of requirements, ranked as must-have or nice-to-have; a spreadsheet that works out the three-year total cost of ownership of each option, checked twice; a weighted scoring matrix with agreed criteria and weights adding to 100%; a risk register covering at least power and internet outages, data protection, security and supplier failure; and a two-page recommendation report to the owners. Give each member a named role: requirements analyst, cost analyst (total cost of ownership), scoring lead (criteria, weights and matrix), risk and compliance lead (risk register), and report writer (who also checks that the figures in the report match the spreadsheets). In a group of four, the scoring lead also prepares the risk register. Each member explains their part to the assessor.
materials: Case pack from the assessor: business profile, problem, three product fact sheets and quotations
Computers with spreadsheet and word-processing software
Flipchart paper and markers for planning
photos: The total cost of ownership spreadsheet on screen
The weighted scoring matrix on screen
The group explaining the recommendation to the assessor
checklist: Took a named role and completed their part of the evidence
Requirements come from the business need, not from product features
Total cost figures are complete and correctly worked out
Criteria and weights are sensible and the scores are applied correctly
Risks are realistic for the business and have controls
The recommendation follows from the evidence and is clearly written
Explained their part and answered the assessor's questions
safety: Use only the made-up case, products and prices; do not name real brands
Keep the case pack and the group's work confidential to the group and assessor
Respect every member's view when agreeing weights and scores
Share the workload fairly and take short screen breaks

practical2.title: Run a proof-of-concept test of an online tool and present a go or no-go decision (role play)
practical2.brief: The assessor sets up a free or trial online tool on Centre computers, using a Centre account (for example an online form builder, an appointment booking tool or a shared task board), and gives your group a business scenario, such as a hair salon in Montego Bay that wants online bookings. As a group, plan and run a proof of concept to decide whether the tool meets the business's needs, and produce: a test plan with five or more test tasks, success measures and the baseline time for doing each task the current way; a test log recording the time taken, problems found and a screenshot for each task; user feedback from two members of another group who try the tool and fill in a short feedback form; and a five-slide presentation to a management panel (the assessor) giving a go, go-with-changes or no-go decision with reasons. Give each member a named role: test planner, tester (carries out the tasks), recorder (times each task and keeps the log and screenshots), user feedback lead (runs the user trial and summarises the forms), and presenter. In a group of four, the recorder also leads the user feedback. Every member presents their part of the findings.
materials: Centre computers with internet access and a Centre trial account set up by the assessor
Feedback forms and test log templates
photos: The test plan with tasks, measures and baseline times
Screenshots of the tool during at least three test tasks
The user feedback forms being filled in
The presentation to the management panel, with the slides showing
checklist: Took a named role and completed their part of the evidence
Test tasks reflect the business's real needs
Times and problems are recorded accurately for each task
User feedback was gathered fairly and summarised honestly
The decision follows from the evidence and names conditions or risks
Presented their part clearly and within time
Followed the Centre's rules for computer and account use
safety: Enter no real personal data; use made-up names and test details only
Use only the Centre account the assessor set up and do not accept new terms or payments
Log out of the tool and close the browser at the end of the session
Take regular screen breaks and sit at the computer comfortably
